findings.claim: All 14 lessons set questions in forms this paper does not use for a British depth study: 26 x '4 marks - Describe Two Features', 24 x '8 marks - Explain Significance', 14 x '16 marks - Period Argument', 13 x '8 marks - Explain Effects' and 4 x '4 marks - Two Ways Similar or Different'. Not one lesson set an interpretation question, and the section's first question is an interpretation question.
findings.truth: Section B of this paper sets four compulsory questions on the depth study: an 8-mark interpretation question ('How convincing is Interpretation A about ...'), an 8-mark 'Explain what was important about ...', an 8-mark 'Write an account of ...' and the 16-mark essay on the specified site (spec 4.4.2 table and the notes under it). 'Describe two features' and 'Explain the significance of' belong to other papers and to the thematic-study section; the comparison question is not set on this content and is 8 marks, not 4. Every question was converted to one of the real forms with a rebuilt mark scheme, so each lesson now carries one interpretation question, three or two 'what was important' questions and two or one accounts.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Paper 2 Section B table (question types, marks, AO4 on the interpretation question)

findings.claim: The site essays in lessons 13 and 14 were typed '16 marks - Period Argument' and their mark schemes gave no tariff line and no SPaG marks.
findings.truth: The 16-mark question is the historic-environment essay on the specified site and it carries 4 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. Retyped, with the tariff and a band ladder added; the same SPaG fact added to the lesson text of both site lessons.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Section B table; 2.2 Assessments (84 marks including 4 for SPaG)

findings.claim: 'In 1066 there were perhaps fifty castles in the whole of England. By 1100 there were close to five hundred.' Repeated in the key fact, the conclusion and a flashcard.
findings.truth: England had only a handful of castles before 1066 - those built in the 1050s by Norman knights in Edward the Confessor's service (Hereford, Clavering, Richard's Castle, probably Ewyas Harold), which is what this lesson's own next paragraph says. About fifty is the Domesday figure for 1086, not for 1066.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Castles in Great Britain and Ireland'; Wikipedia, 'Castle' (castles introduced into England shortly before 1066)

findings.claim: 'For a 4-mark ‘Two Ways Similar or Different’ question on Anglo-Saxon and Norman government ...'
findings.truth: This paper sets no comparison question on the British depth study; the thematic-study comparison question is 8 marks. Recast as the 'explain what was important' question this content is actually examined by.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Section A and Section B tables

findings.claim: 'For a 4-mark ‘Two Ways Similar or Different’ question on Anglo-Saxon and Norman daily life ...'
findings.truth: Same error as F37; recast for the account question.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Section A and Section B tables

findings.claim: 'King Edward the Confessor died in his new abbey church at Westminster.'
findings.truth: Edward died at his palace at Westminster. He was too ill even to attend the consecration of the new abbey church on 28 December 1065; he was buried in it on 6 January 1066.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Edward the Confessor'

findings.claim: 'his brothers Tostig, Gyrth and Leofwine held Northumbria, East Anglia and Kent' - given as Harold's power base in January 1066.
findings.truth: Tostig had been driven out of Northumbria in the revolt of 1065 and Morcar held it; the same lesson says so four paragraphs later. Only Gyrth and Leofwine still held earldoms.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction; spec Part one (revolts and claimants)

findings.claim: Description ends mid-sentence: 'and why Norman victory was.'
findings.truth: Completed to 'and why Norman victory was close-run', which is the lesson's argument.
findings.evidence: the field itself

findings.claim: 'Harold heard the news in London around 21 September.' The same lesson has him covering 185 miles in four to five days and reaching Tadcaster on 24 September.
findings.truth: The march took about four days, so Harold cannot have left London on 21 September; he heard of the invasion in mid-September. The precise date is removed rather than replaced with another guess.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Stamford Bridge' (185 miles from London to Yorkshire in four days)

findings.claim: Description ends mid-sentence: 'submissions, castles and the Christmas.'
findings.truth: Completed to 'a Christmas coronation'.
findings.evidence: the field itself

findings.claim: William was crowned 'on the spot where Harold had been crowned the year before'.
findings.truth: Harold was crowned on 6 January 1066 and William on 25 December 1066 - the same year. 'The year before' invites students to date Harold's coronation to 1065.
findings.evidence: spec Part one; Wikipedia, 'Edward the Confessor'

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'How long after landing did William fortify Dover Castle?' - 'Eight days.'
findings.truth: The eight days is the time William spent strengthening Dover, not the gap between landing and fortifying it. Question reworded.
findings.evidence: lesson content ('Dover's castle was strengthened in eight days')

findings.claim: Fens definition (in the dfn and the glossary): '... before drainage in the 17th century made the wetlands hard to penetrate by an army.'
findings.truth: The opposite: the wetland was hard to cross before it was drained. The sentence was garbled and taught the reverse of the point the lesson needs.
findings.evidence: internal logic; lesson content on the causeways at Ely

findings.claim: 'a Danish fleet of around 240 ships under Sweyn II of Denmark ... sailed up the Humber' (also in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Sweyn II sent the 1069 fleet but did not sail with it; it was commanded by his sons. Sweyn came to England in person only in 1070.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Harrying of the North'

findings.claim: Orderic Vitalis 'records William reportedly saying he would ‘not lay down his arms until I have brought the rebels to such submission as they shall never forget’.'
findings.truth: The quotation could not be found in Orderic and mixes third and first person inside one set of quotation marks. Rewritten as reported speech, which is what the chronicle supports.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Harrying of the North' (the Orderic passages quoted there are different)

findings.claim: John of Worcester's chronicle is 'one of the main contemporary sources for William's reign and the Harrying' (dfn and glossary); a practice question asked for 'contemporary chronicle evidence'.
findings.truth: John of Worcester died in 1140 and wrote decades after the Harrying, as this lesson itself stresses. He is a later narrative source, not a contemporary one.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own glossary dates; spec Part one

findings.claim: 'Robert of Mortain alone held nearly 800 manors across thirteen counties' - repeated in a collapsible, a knowledge check, a mark scheme and a flashcard.
findings.truth: Domesday gives him 797 manors spread across twenty counties.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Robert, Count of Mortain'

findings.claim: 'Other stone keeps followed at Colchester ..., at Lincoln, and at Rochester' between 1066 and 1100 (also in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Lincoln had no stone keep before 1100 - its curtain wall predates 1115 and the Lucy Tower is 12th century. Rochester's famous keep is William de Corbeil's, about 1127; the work that belongs in this period is Bishop Gundulf's stone castle of 1087-89.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Rochester Castle'; Wikipedia, 'Lincoln Castle'

findings.claim: 'Castles, the Chronicler complained, ‘filled the country’' - quoted as the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle on Norman castles, with a flashcard built on the phrase.
findings.truth: The famous 'filled the land full of castles' passage is the Chronicle's 1137 annal on Stephen's reign, not on William's. The Chronicle's complaint for 1066-67 is that castles were built far and wide and the poor were oppressed. The quotation marks are removed and the substance kept.
findings.evidence: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1137 annal (Peterborough) vs the 1066-67 annals; the wording could not be verified for this period

findings.claim: 'Understanding what was kept and what was added is the way to answer the spec's comparison questions cleanly.'
findings.truth: There is no comparison question on the British depth study; this content is examined through change, continuity, causation and consequence.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Section B notes on questions 2 and 3

findings.claim: 'The historian Hugh Thomas calls this ‘continuity beneath rupture’' - repeated as a quotation in lesson 10 and in a flashcard in each lesson.
findings.truth: The phrase could not be verified as Thomas's wording. His argument (English continuity beneath a transformed ruling class) is kept; the quotation marks and the 'he calls it' framing are removed.
findings.evidence: no source found for the phrase in Hugh Thomas, The English and the Normans (2003)

findings.claim: 'the fine survived ... until the 12th century, when intermarriage made it impossible to tell Normans and English apart and the procedure was effectively abandoned.'
findings.truth: The Dialogue of the Exchequer (about 1179) does say the two peoples could no longer be told apart, but the murdrum fine was profitable and presentment of Englishry was only abolished by statute in 1340.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Presentment of Englishry' (Engleschrie Act 1340)

findings.claim: 'the wave of new foundations from Battle (1067) through Selby (1069)' (also dated 1067 in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: William's penance was imposed by Pope Alexander II in 1070 and building at Battle began after that; the church was finished about 1094.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Battle Abbey'

findings.claim: Description is 137 characters.
findings.truth: Over the length the validator allows (60-120). Shortened to 86.
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py

findings.claim: 'examiners reward causal links rather than dates in a row'
findings.truth: Invented exam claim. Rewritten as advice about what a strong answer does. Nine more of these were found and removed: F8 (L2 'the highest band rewards'), F12 (L3 'examiners reward two precise features'), F19 (L4 'Examiners reward causal links between specific events and specific policies'), F22 (L5 'as the AQA mark schemes and examiner reports consistently reward', plus a heading 'What examiners want when you discuss numbers'), F23 (L5 'Examiners reward students who weigh both moments'), F26 (L6 'examiner reports reward those who can describe'), F27 (L6 'Examiners reward causal links, not labelled diagrams'), F33 (L7 'the examiner wants two precise features' and 'score nothing'), F36 (L8 'AQA examiners reward students who can hold both readings together'), F37/F42 (L8, L10), F39 (L9), F43 (L11), F45 (L12) and F47 (L13 'the examiner wants something specific').
findings.evidence: no published source states what examiners reward in these terms; house copyright-distancing rule

findings.claim: Harold 'shipwrecked on the Norman coast in around 1064'.
findings.truth: He was wrecked on the coast of Ponthieu and held by Count Guy before William obtained him; the oath itself was sworn in Normandy.
findings.evidence: standard account of the 1064 journey (Bayeux Tapestry sequence)

findings.claim: 'William ordered one built at Hastings within hours of landing.'
findings.truth: William landed at Pevensey and fortified it there; the Hastings castle went up after he moved his base, within days. Lesson 2 says the same.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with lesson 2

findings.claim: One-word answer 'Wessex.'; question 'On what year did William claim ...'
findings.truth: Answer given a fuller form; 'On what year' corrected to 'In what year'.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules (a one-word answer needs a fuller answer)

findings.claim: List answers that fail the flashcard validator's enumeration rule: L2 'Archers, infantry and mounted knights.' (F9), L3 'Edgar Atheling, alongside Edwin, Morcar and the leading bishops.' and 'Through Romney, Dover, Canterbury, Wallingford and Berkhamsted.' (F13), L4 'Castles at Warwick, Nottingham, York and Lincoln.' (F20), L5 'Yorkshire, with severe destruction also in Durham, Cheshire and the Tees valley.' and 'Villages, livestock and stored grain ...' (F24), L6 'William's coalition included Normans, Bretons, Flemings and French.' (F28), L9 'The smaller, fuller volume covering Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex.' (F40), L10 'It removed customary rights to firewood, game and grazing ...' (F41), L12 'Latin (Church and chancery), Anglo-Norman (lords), Old English (peasants).' (F46).
findings.truth: Each rewritten as a single idea that passes the validator and still tests something worth knowing.
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py, FC_ENUM_PATTERN

findings.claim: Description ends mid-sentence: 'that nearly unmade.'
findings.truth: Completed to 'that nearly unmade the conquest'.
findings.evidence: the field itself

findings.claim: 'the 16-mark question will reward you for reading it like a document' - the SPaG marks are not mentioned in either site lesson.
findings.truth: The site question carries 4 SPaG marks on top of the 16. Added to both site lessons.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2

findings.claim: Lessons 1-12 each carried a 16-mark 'Period Argument' essay. The only 16-mark question this section sets is the historic-environment essay on the specified site, so these were converted to the 8-mark interpretation question (their support/against bullets already had the right shape).
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. (a) What I did: content lessons practise the three 8-mark forms and the 16-mark essay lives only in lessons 13 and 14, which is what the exam does. (b) The alternative: keep a 16-mark question in every lesson but tie each one to the specified site, so students get more extended-writing practice - at the cost of asking site questions in lessons that do not teach the site. Recommendation: keep (a), and if Tom wants more extended-writing practice, add site-linked 16-markers to lessons 13 and 14 rather than to the content lessons.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2 Section B table (the 16-mark question is the site essay)
findings.ruling: Accepted: 16-mark practice sits on the site lessons (13-14) only; extended-writing drills for L1-12 are a later build item.

findings.claim: Orderic Vitalis is called 'the Norman chronicler' in the body and in a knowledge check, while the lesson's own glossary calls him Anglo-Norman.
findings.truth: He was born in Shropshire in 1075 to a Norman father and an English mother and became a monk at Saint-Evroul. 'Norman chronicler' is defensible for where he wrote but sits oddly beside the glossary and slightly overstates the 'even the Normans condemned it' point. Left alone to avoid churn.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own glossary entry

findings.claim: The move of the see from Dorchester to Lincoln is listed among the relocations ordered at the 1075 council of London.
findings.truth: The 1075 council decreed the moves of Sherborne, Selsey and Lichfield. Remigius had already moved Dorchester to Lincoln in about 1072, though the council is often said to have confirmed it. Contested, and it appears in five places, so it is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: council of London 1075 decrees

findings.claim: 'The New Forest in Hampshire was created by clearing villages of their inhabitants' (also lesson 10).
findings.truth: This is the chronicle tradition and standard GCSE teaching. Modern landscape work argues the soils were poor and the area thinly settled, so the scale of eviction is disputed. Not wrong enough to edit.
findings.evidence: historiography of the New Forest afforestation

findings.claim: 'A wooden castle could be thrown up in a fortnight.'
findings.truth: True of small ones and of what contemporaries claimed; archaeologists estimate four to nine months for the larger mottes (Thetford needed roughly 24,000 man-days).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Motte-and-bailey castle'

findings.claim: The survey 'produced two volumes of Latin in less than nine months'.
findings.truth: The fieldwork was that fast; the writing-up of Great Domesday ran on beyond August 1086. The sentence overstates slightly.
findings.evidence: standard accounts of the compilation

findings.claim: Lessons 13 and 14 carry only 5 flashcards each and 5 MCQ knowledge checks each.
findings.truth: The validator wants at least 6 flashcards and a mixed knowledge-check set (2 MCQ plus fill and match). A build gap, not a fact error, and adding items is outside the scope of an edits file.
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py

findings.claim: Lessons 13 and 14 use unicode punctuation (curly apostrophes, em dashes) inside *_html fields.
findings.truth: House convention is entities in *_html. Cosmetic; renders correctly.
findings.evidence: project conventions

findings.claim: The 14 new interpretation questions need an Interpretation A.
findings.truth: Each one is composed for the exercise and says so in its first line ('an interpretation written for this exercise'). No historian's name, publication or archive provenance is attached to any of them, and no existing source in the unit was invented.
findings.evidence: house rule on composed sources

findings.claim: Lessons 13 and 14 claim the Battle of Hastings is the 2027 specified site and the White Tower the 2028 site.
findings.truth: Both correct. AQA's published list for Norman England gives Pevensey Castle (2026), the Battle of Hastings (2027) and the White Tower (2028), so the unit is aimed correctly at the cohort now sitting the course.
findings.evidence: aqa.org.uk news item 'GCSE History: Historic environment sites 2026-2028'

summary: No lesson was clean: the exam furniture was wrong across the whole unit. All 84 practice questions were set in forms this paper does not use for a British depth study - 26 four-mark 'describe two features', 24 thematic-study significance questions, 14 sixteen-mark 'period arguments', 13 'explain effects' and 4 four-mark comparisons - and no lesson set the interpretation question that opens the section. Every question was converted to the four real forms with rebuilt mark schemes and a labelled, composed Interpretation A per lesson, and the site essays were retyped with their SPaG marks. Alongside that: 15 fifteen invented examiner or mark-scheme claims removed, one HIGH factual error (England had a handful of castles in 1066, not fifty), and MEDIUM corrections to Edward's place of death, Tostig's earldom in January 1066, Harold's march date, William's coronation 'the year before', the garbled Fens definition, the command of the 1069 Danish fleet, an unverifiable Orderic quotation, John of Worcester as a 'contemporary' source, Robert of Mortain's twenty counties, the Lincoln and Rochester stone keeps, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 'filled the country' quotation (which belongs to 1137), the 'continuity beneath rupture' quotation attributed to Hugh Thomas, the murdrum fine's abolition in 1340, Battle Abbey's foundation date, three descriptions that broke off mid-sentence and one over-length description. 325 edits, one ADJUDICATE (whether content lessons should keep a 16-mark question at all) and nine NOTEs. The 2027 and 2028 specified sites were verified against AQA's published list and are correct.
